title: Getting Started with Playwright
excerpt: Let's set up Playwright from scratch and write our first automated test.
html:
Step 1: Create a Project Folder

Open your terminal and create a new folder for your Playwright project.

mkdir playwright-fundamentals

Now move into the project folder.

cd playwright-fundamentals

From this point onward, every command should be executed inside this folder.

Step 2: Install Playwright

The Playwright team provides excellent documentation, and it's always a good idea to keep it bookmarked.

Official Documentation: https://playwright.dev/docs/intro

Now install Playwright by running:

npm init playwright@latest

Playwright will ask you a few questions during the installation.

Let's go through them together.

Choose a Language

You'll first be asked:

Which language would you like to use?

Select:

TypeScript

Then press Enter.

Since we've already learned TypeScript, we'll continue using it throughout this series.

Choose the Test Folder

Next you'll see:

Where should your tests be placed?

Keep the default value.

tests

Press Enter.

Playwright will create a tests folder where we'll keep all of our test files.

Add a GitHub Actions Workflow

You'll then be asked:

Add a GitHub Actions workflow?

Select:

No

We'll learn GitHub Actions later after we've covered the Playwright fundamentals.

Install Playwright Browsers

Finally you'll see:

Install Playwright browsers?

Select:

Yes

Playwright will now download the browser binaries required for automation. This may take a few minutes depending on your internet connection. Once the installation is complete, your project is ready.

Step 3: Open the Project in Visual Studio Code

Run:

code .

The . simply means open the current folder.

Visual Studio Code should now open your Playwright project.

Step 4: Install the Playwright Extension

Before writing any tests, let's install the official Playwright extension for Visual Studio Code.

Open the Extensions panel in VS Code and search for:

Playwright Test for VSCode

Install the extension published by Microsoft.

The extension provides several useful features, including:

  • Running individual tests directly from the editor.

  • Debugging tests.

  • Viewing test results.

  • Quick access to Playwright commands.

We'll start using these features as we progress through the series.

Step 5: Understanding the Project Structure

After installation, your project should look similar to this.

playwright-fundamentals/
│
├── node_modules/
├── tests/
├── playwright.config.ts
├── package.json
├── package-lock.json
└── .gitignore

Don't worry about every file right now.

Let's look at the important ones.

tests/

This is where all of our test files will live.

Throughout this series, I'll ask you to create a new test file whenever we begin a new topic.

This keeps related examples together and makes your project much easier to navigate later.

playwright.config.ts

This is Playwright's main configuration file.

It controls things like:

  • Browser settings

  • Timeouts

  • Retries

  • Base URL

  • Reporters

We'll customize this file later in the series.

package.json

This file contains information about your project and its dependencies.

As we install more tools throughout the series, you'll notice this file updating automatically.

Step 6: Run the Sample Tests

Before writing our own code, let's make sure everything was installed correctly.

Open the terminal and run:

npx playwright test

Let's understand this command.

  • npx runs a package without installing it globally.

  • playwright is the package we're using.

  • test tells Playwright to execute all test files it finds inside the tests folder.

If everything is configured correctly, you should see the sample tests pass.

Congratulations! Your Playwright environment is now ready.

Step 7: Create Your First Test File

Although Playwright generates sample tests during installation, we'll create our own file so you can understand how everything works.

Inside the tests folder, create a new file named:

getting-started.spec.ts

We'll continue using this approach throughout the series. Every major topic will have its own dedicated test file.

Step 8: Write Your First Playwright Test

Open getting-started.spec.ts and add the following code.

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("Open the Playwright website", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://playwright.dev");

  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/Playwright/);
});

Save the file.

Now open your terminal and run:

npx playwright test tests/getting-started.spec.ts

This command tells Playwright to execute only the test inside getting-started.spec.ts.

If everything is working correctly, the test should pass.

Congratulations! You've just written and executed your first Playwright test.

Understanding the Test

Let's look at the code one section at a time.

Importing Playwright

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

This imports two important Playwright functions.

  • test() is used to create a test.

  • expect() is used to verify the result.

You'll use these in almost every Playwright test.

Creating a Test

test("Open the Playwright website", async ({ page }) => {

This creates a new test. The first value is simply the test name.

Choose names that clearly describe what the test is doing. Good test names make reports much easier to read.

The page object represents a browser tab. Every action we perform will happen through this object.

Opening a Website

await page.goto("https://playwright.dev");

This tells Playwright to open the Playwright website.

The await keyword waits until the page has loaded before moving to the next line. page.goto() tells Playwright to open a webpage in the browser. You'll usually start almost every Playwright test with page.goto() because your test needs to open a page before it can interact with it.

Verifying the Page

await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/Playwright/);

This is called an assertion. expect() is used to verify that something happened as expected. toHaveTitle() checks the title of the current webpage. The / / means "contains". It tells Playwright to look for a word instead of matching the entire text. So, /Playwright/ means "Look for the word 'Playwright' in the page title."

Think of it as asking a question.

"Is the page title correct?"

If the answer is Yes, the test passes. If the answer is No, the test fails.

Automation isn't just about interacting with a website. It's also about verifying that the application behaves as expected.

Practice

Now it's your turn.

Create a new test that opens the GitHub homepage and verifies that the page title contains the word GitHub.

Follow these steps:

  1. Rename the test to something meaningful, such as "Open the GitHub website".

  2. Replace the URL with the GitHub homepage.

  3. Update the expected page title to match the new website.

  4. Run the test from the terminal.

  5. Check whether the test passes successfully.

If your test passes, you've successfully written your first Playwright test using a different website.

Practice Answer:

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("Open the GitHub website", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://github.com");

  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/GitHub/);
});

Useful Commands for Running Tests

As you start working with Playwright, you'll often use a few command-line options to control how your tests run. Here are two of the most common ones.

Run Tests in a Specific Browser

npx playwright test --project=chromium

The --project=chromium option tells Playwright to run your tests only in the Chromium browser.
By default, Playwright may run tests in multiple browsers. This option is useful when you want to test or debug in a single browser.

Run Tests with a Visible Browser

npx playwright test --headed

By default, Playwright runs tests in headless mode, which means the browser runs in the background without opening a browser window.

The --headed option opens a visible browser window so you can watch your test execute step by step. This is especially helpful while you're learning Playwright or debugging a test.

Combine Both Options

npx playwright test --project=chromium --headed

This command tells Playwright to:

  • Run the test only in the Chromium browser.

  • Open the browser window so you can watch the test run.

So, If you want to run only your getting-started.spec.ts test in a visible Chromium browser, use:

npx playwright test tests/getting-started.spec.ts --project=chromium --headed

  1. npx → Runs the Playwright package.

  2. playwright test → Starts the Playwright test runner.

  3. tests/getting-started.spec.ts → Runs only this test file.

  4. --project=chromium → Uses the Chromium browser.

  5. --headed → Opens a visible browser window so you can watch the test run.

You'll use these options frequently throughout this series, so it's worth getting familiar with them early.
